name: Jeremiah
v: In the seventh month, Ishmael son of Nethaniah, son of Elishama — royal blood, one of the king's officers — came to Gedaliah son of Ahikam at Mizpah with ten men. They sat down to a meal together.

Then Ishmael and his ten men rose from the table, drew their swords, and cut down Gedaliah son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan — the man the king of Babylon had appointed over the land. They killed him there.
Ishmael also killed every Judean with Gedaliah at Mizpah, and the Babylonian soldiers stationed there — the warriors.
The day after the murder, before anyone knew,
eighty men arrived from Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria — beards shaved, clothes torn, bodies gashed — carrying grain offerings and incense to bring to the house of the Lord.
Ishmael went out from Mizpah to meet them, weeping as he walked. When he reached them, he said, "Come — come to Gedaliah son of Ahikam."
But the moment they were inside the town, Ishmael and his men slaughtered them and threw their bodies into a cistern.
Ten of them, though, said to Ishmael, "Don't kill us — we have stores hidden in the field: wheat, barley, oil, honey." So he held back and didn't kill them with the others.

The cistern where Ishmael dumped every corpse of the men he struck down — bodies thrown in with Gedaliah's — was the one King Asa had dug long ago as a defense against Baasha king of Israel. Ishmael son of Nethaniah filled it with the slain.

Then Ishmael took captive everyone left in Mizpah — the king's daughters and all the people Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had entrusted to Gedaliah son of Ahikam. Ishmael son of Nethaniah took them and set out to cross over to the Ammonites.
When Johanan son of Kareah and all the army officers with him heard about every atrocity Ishmael son of Nethaniah had committed,
they gathered all their men and went out to fight Ishmael son of Nethaniah. They caught up with him at the great pool in Gibeon.
When all the people Ishmael was holding saw Johanan son of Kareah and the army officers with him, they were overjoyed.
Every captive Ishmael had taken from Mizpah turned around and ran back to Johanan son of Kareah.
But Ishmael son of Nethaniah broke away from Johanan with eight men and escaped to the Ammonites.

Then Johanan son of Kareah and the army officers with him gathered up the rest of the people Ishmael son of Nethaniah had taken from Mizpah after killing Gedaliah son of Ahikam — soldiers, women, children, and court officials — bringing them back from Gibeon.
They moved on and stopped at Geruth Kimham near Bethlehem, intending to push on to Egypt —
away from the Babylonians. They were terrified of them, because Ishmael son of Nethaniah had killed Gedaliah son of Ahikam, the man the king of Babylon had set over the land.

com.d:
# Jeremiah 41: Tragedy and the Struggle to Trust God's Word

This chapter shows us the devastating aftermath of refusing to listen to God's messenger, and how fear can paralyze faith even when God has promised protection. After the fall of Jerusalem, a remnant of people under Gedaliah's leadership had begun rebuilding, but tragedy strikes when the ambitious Ishmael assassinates Gedaliah and takes the survivors hostage. The chaos unfolds with graphic brutality—Ishmael slaughters eighty pilgrims and throws their bodies into a cistern, then captures the royal family and remaining inhabitants, intending to defect to the Ammonites.

What makes this account spiritually significant is how it echoes the pattern of the entire book. God had sent Jeremiah repeatedly to warn against political resistance and to call people toward surrender to Babylon's rule. Though Jerusalem fell and many died, God had promised that a remnant would survive and find hope. Yet here, when that remnant begins tentatively rebuilding under Gedaliah's leadership, internal betrayal and violence nearly destroy what remained. Johanan, a military commander, discovers Ishmael's treachery and rescues the captives—but then his response reveals the spiritual crisis underneath.

The deeper tragedy is what happens next: fearing Babylonian retaliation, Johanan and the others decide to flee to Egypt, directly violating God's earlier instruction through Jeremiah not to do precisely this. Despite everything they've witnessed, despite having a prophet among them still speaking God's word, they choose self-protection over obedience. They are so traumatized, so convinced that their strategy is the only way forward, that they cannot trust that God might work through surrender rather than escape.

This speaks to our own struggles with faith. When life shatters us, our instinctive response is often to seize control rather than trust God's unfolding plan. We've been wounded by events beyond our control, and our fear shouts louder than God's promises.

What area of your life have you stopped trusting God with because of past pain or present uncertainty?
com.s:
Jeremiah 41 narrates one of the most tragic episodes in the aftermath of Jerusalem's fall to Babylon in 586 BCE, recounting the assassination of Gedaliah, the Babylonian-appointed governor of Judah, and its catastrophic consequences for the remnant community. This chapter continues the prose narrative that dominates the latter portions of Jeremiah, likely compiled by Baruch or later editors drawing upon historical memory preserved among the Judean survivors. The events transpire approximately two months after the temple's destruction, during a period when the remaining population might have hoped for stability under Gedaliah's administration at Mizpah.

The perpetrator, Ishmael son of Nethaniah, bears significant credentials as a member of the royal family (*mizzera' hammelûkāh*), suggesting his actions were motivated partly by dynastic ambition and resentment toward Babylonian authority. His collaboration with Baalis, king of the Ammonites, indicates the broader regional political machinations surrounding Judah's collapse. The verb *nākāh* (to strike, kill) appears repeatedly throughout the chapter, emphasizing the relentless violence that characterized this period. Ishmael's treachery during a shared meal violates fundamental ancient Near Eastern conventions of hospitality and covenantal fellowship, rendering his actions particularly heinous within the cultural framework.

The slaughter of eighty pilgrims from the former northern territories—Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria—arriving with grain offerings and incense for the ruined temple site presents interpretive challenges. Their shaved beards, torn garments, and self-laceration indicate mourning practices, some of which later pentateuchal legislation would prohibit. Their journey suggests that Yahwistic worship continued despite the temple's destruction, and Ishmael's massacre of these worshippers deepens the portrait of his depravity.

The chapter concludes with Johanan son of Kareah's rescue of the captives Ishmael had seized, though Ishmael himself escapes to Ammon. The remnant's encampment at Geruth Chimham near Bethlehem, positioned for potential flight to Egypt, foreshadows the disobedience recounted in subsequent chapters. Theologically, this narrative demonstrates how human violence and political calculation continued to undermine any possibility of restoration in the land, setting the stage for the Egyptian exile that Jeremiah had explicitly warned against.
com.p:
This chapter records events that occurred in 586 BC, immediately following the destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar's Babylonian forces. The temple lay in ruins, the Davidic monarchy had been toppled, and only a remnant of the poorest remained in the land under Gedaliah, a governor appointed by Babylon. Within the grand redemptive arc, this passage belongs to the darkest hour of Israel's exile—the covenant curses of Deuteronomy fully realized, the visible kingdom apparently extinguished, yet standing paradoxically at the threshold of restoration promises that prophets like Jeremiah himself had proclaimed.

The assassination of Gedaliah by Ishmael, a man of royal blood, represents the final tragic convulsion of a dying order. Here is the seed of David's house turned murderer rather than shepherd, slaying the very governor who offered the remnant a path of humble survival. Ishmael's treachery carries profound typological weight as an anti-David figure—whereas David spared Saul and refused to grasp kingship through violence, Ishmael seizes through bloodshed what he believes belongs to him by lineage. His massacre of innocent pilgrims journeying to worship at the temple ruins reveals the utter corruption of those who claimed covenant privilege while practicing covenant abomination.

The eighty mourners from Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria traveling with grain offerings and incense demonstrate that even after catastrophic judgment, hearts still yearned for Zion. They came with torn clothes and gashed bodies, mourning the house of the Lord. Their slaughter at Ishmael's hand typifies the fate of sincere worshipers caught in the crossfire of political violence—a foreshadowing of how the faithful would suffer throughout Israel's history until another royal son would be murdered, not to destroy the remnant but to gather it.

Johanan's rescue of the captives from Ishmael points dimly toward future deliverance, yet the rescue remains incomplete, overshadowed by fear rather than faith. The remnant now camps near Bethlehem, poised to flee to Egypt against the explicit word of the Lord. Near Bethlehem—the very soil from which David arose and from which, six centuries later, David's greater Son would emerge.

For the church dwelling between the advents, this blood-soaked chapter testifies that human scheming cannot thwart divine purpose. Empires fall, governors are murdered, and remnants scatter, yet God preserves a people through judgment unto restoration. The chaos of human history remains firmly within the sovereign hand that brings forth Messiah from apparent ruin.
